dilemmas.dilemma_description: An employee learns that a colleague has submitted falsified safety data concerning a widely used product. Disclosing the information may prevent future risk to users but could result in professional consequences for the colleague, disruption within the organization, and potential retaliation against the employee. Choosing not to disclose maintains existing professional relationships and organizational stability but leaves a latent risk unaddressed. The employee must decide what to do, and why.

The student genuinely needs the money and is academically deserving, but others with accurate documentation were rejected. Reporting the fraud could destroy the student's future, while ignoring it undermines fairness and trust in the process. The counselor must decide what to do, and why.

research_notes.purpose: To run a Yoruba-first version of the deixis experiment while reusing the published English article sessions as the fixed comparison baseline.
research_notes.translation_policy: When translations are needed, use smoother academic English while preserving deictic stance and ethical reasoning.
research_notes.analysis_note: The current analysis pipeline remains English-oriented, so translated Yoruba responses are expected to serve as the first analysis-facing layer.

methodological_typology.rationale: Yoruba grammaticalizes deictic anchoring through aspect (ti, ń, máa ń), focus (ni), and existential (wà) particles that have no clean English equivalents. After audit-driven normalization, the six impersonal Yoruba cells are NOT homogeneous with respect to deictic anchoring. Analysis should not pool them as a single condition; it should distinguish three subtypes. Likewise, non-impersonal Yoruba cells carry residual deictic encoding (existential wà, progressive ń) that their English counterparts do not. This block makes those distinctions explicit and machine-readable for downstream analysis.

impersonal_subtype_definitions.bare_perfective: Impersonal opening uses bare perfective verbs without overt ti perfect marking. Speaker-now anchoring is minimised. Closest available Yoruba match to the English neutral-narrative impersonal.
impersonal_subtype_definitions.progressive_background: Impersonal opening uses ń progressive in a background clause (e.g. nígbà tí ó ń tọ́jú). The progressive is anchored to narrative time, not to a speaker now, but it adds a vivid present-tense-like frame relative to English.
impersonal_subtype_definitions.double_progressive_irreducible: Impersonal opening uses double ń progressive (e.g. ń sáré ń sún mọ́). Structurally required to describe an ongoing event. Carries higher implicit proximal deixis than the English counterpart. Treat as an irreducible typological residual.
impersonal_subtype_definitions.bare_perfective_with_habitual: Impersonal opening uses bare perfective for the main change-of-state event but retains máa ń habitual for the repeated AI behaviour, which is semantically necessary.
impersonal_subtype_definitions.existential_stative_restructured: Impersonal opening was rewritten to avoid the presentational focus particle ni. Stative descriptions of patient distress still use tó wà existential, which is unavoidable in natural Yoruba.

residual_deictic_encoding_outside_impers.reflexive: Opening uses Mo rí ara mi tí mo wà nítòsí ..., which locates the speaker in the scene via the existential wà. The English reflexive (I find myself ...) does not require this overt locative.
residual_deictic_encoding_outside_impers.spatial: Adds Níbí ... Láti ipò yìí, which is the closest Yoruba mapping of the English here/there/from this position contrast.
